tells.1: “With time for work and time for care” adds a conspicuously balanced slogan to an otherwise practical instruction.
tells.3: “With time for work and time for care” feels manufactured; “Make time for your work” is generic.
tells.4: The closing “you see the price before you book” unnecessarily explains what the displayed price already accomplishes.
tells.5: Repeated explanatory endings—“nothing separate to arrange” and “so you know the price”—overwork straightforward information.
tells.6: The balanced opening and abstract “time set aside for work and care” give the copy a formulaic marketing polish.
tells.7: “With time for work and time for care” supplies decorative symmetry without useful information.

reason: Version 4 is the most direct, restrained and credible, with practical headings and little decorative language. Version 2 may feel human in its roughness, but its errors and awkward formatting make it the least convincing example of skilled landing-page writing; these judgments concern style, not proof of authorship.
